title: Stop yourself committing a secret
summary: Write a pre-commit hook that refuses commits containing credentials or huge files. Watch it block a real commit, then learn the flag that bypasses it and why that matters.
mental_model: A hook is an executable in `.git/hooks` named after the event. Git runs it and reads the exit code: zero proceeds, non-zero aborts. That is the entire API.
danger: Hooks are local and bypassable with `--no-verify`. They are a helpful guard rail, never a security control — the server must enforce anything that actually matters.

steps.title: Look at what git offers you
steps.why: Every repository ships with sample hooks, disabled by the `.sample` suffix. Renaming one activates it — there is no registration step and no config to set.
steps.expect: A dozen .sample files, one per hook point.

steps.title: Write a pre-commit hook
steps.why: It inspects the staged content — `diff --cached`, not the working tree — and exits non-zero if it finds a credential pattern or an oversized file. Checking the staged set is the crucial detail: that is what is actually being committed.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Refuse commits containing obvious credentials or large files.

fail=0

if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -nE '^\+.*(AKIA[0-9A-Z]{8,}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----|password[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*["'"'"'][^"'"'"']{6,})' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "pre-commit: refusing to commit what looks like a credential" >&2
  git diff --cached -U0 | grep -nE '^\+.*(AKIA[0-9A-Z]{8,}|password[[:space:]]*=)' >&2
  fail=1
fi

for path in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM); do
  [ -f "$path" ] || continue
  size=$(wc -c < "$path")
  if [ "$size" -gt 100000 ]; then
    echo "pre-commit: $path is ${size} bytes, over the 100000 limit" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done

if [ "$fail" -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "pre-commit: commit aborted. Use --no-verify only if you are certain." >&2
  exit 1
fi

exit 0

steps.title: Try to commit a credential
steps.why: The hook runs before the commit is created, prints its complaint to stderr, and exits 1. Git aborts and nothing enters history — which is the only moment a leak is cheap to fix.
steps.expect: The hook's message, exit code 1, and no new commit.

steps.title: Fix the actual problem
steps.why: Move the secret to an environment variable and the hook passes. The point of a guard rail is that the correct fix is easy and the wrong one is obstructed.

write.content:
import os

AWS_KEY = os.environ['AWS_KEY']
PASSWORD = os.environ['APP_PASSWORD']

commands: git commit -m "Read credentials from the environment"

steps.title: Now the size check
steps.why: The same hook rejects an oversized file. Catching this before the commit is the difference between a two-second fix and a history rewrite later.

verify.label: the oversized file was blocked too

steps.title: The bypass, and what it means
steps.why: `--no-verify` skips client-side hooks entirely. Sometimes legitimate — a hook is wrong, or you are mid-emergency — but it also means a hook can never be your only defence against anything serious.
commands: git commit --no-verify -m "Add binary blob (bypassing the hook)"
steps.expect: The commit succeeds despite the hook, then is undone.

verify.label: the bypassed commit was rolled back afterwards

steps.title: Make it survive a fresh clone
steps.why: `.git/hooks` is not committed and never clones. Keep hooks in a tracked directory and point `core.hooksPath` at it — one config line per clone, and the hooks themselves are reviewed like any other code.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Track the pre-commit hook in the repository"

verify.label: hooks now come from a tracked directory
the hook is tracked so the team can share it
verify.hint: copy it into .githooks, commit, and set core.hooksPath

verify.label: core.hooksPath points at the tracked directory
only the legitimate commits made it into history
verify.hint: the credential and oversized-file commits should have been blocked

verify.label: no credential ever reached a commit

pitfalls: Check `git diff --cached`, not the working tree. A hook that scans working-tree files misses partially staged changes and flags things you never staged.
`--no-verify` bypasses every client-side hook. Anything that must not happen needs a server-side check as well.
Hooks must be executable. On Unix a missing +x makes git skip the hook silently — no error, no protection.
A slow pre-commit hook trains people to use `--no-verify` habitually. Keep it under a second, and put the heavy checks in pre-push or CI.
cheatsheet: runs before a commit is created
